modules.name: Electric Charge and Methods of Charging

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Electro (charge) + statics (rest) = Electrostatics : It is a branch of physics which deals with the study of forces, fields and potential arising from static charges.

Electric Charge : Charge is an intrinsic property associated with matter due to which it produces and experiences, electric and magnetic effects.

Types of charge :

There exist two types of charges in nature.

(1) Positive charge : Due to deficiency of electrons.

(2) Negative charge : Due to excess of electrons.

Units of charge :

SI → coulomb (C)

CGS → stat coulomb (stat C) or e.s.u. of charge

Properties of charge:-

(a) Charge is a scalar quantity.

(b) Like point charges always repel each other while unlike point charges always attract each other.

(c) Charge is transferable:

(d) Charge is always associated with mass

(e) Charge is realistically invariant, whereas mass is variant.

(f) Charge is additive

(g) Charge is conserved

(h) Charge is quantized

Conductors are materials that allow electricity to pass through easily, such as metals, human bodies, and earth.

Insulators are materials that resist the flow of electricity, like glass, rubber, plastic, and wood.

Methods of charging:-

(a) Friction : If we rub one body with another body, electrons get transferred from one body to the another.

Note: Clouds get charged due to friction.

(b) Induction : If a charged body is brought near a neutral body, the charged body will attract opposite charges and repel similar charges present in the neutral body. As a result of this one side of the neutral body becomes negative while the other positive, this process is called 'electrostatic induction'.

In case of induction it is worth noting that :

(1) Inducing body neither gains nor loses charge.

(2) The nature of induced charge is always opposite to that of inducing charge.

(3) Induced charge can be lesser or equal to inducing charge (but never greater).

(4) Induction takes place only in bodies (either conducting or non conducting) and not in particles.

(c) Conduction: Whenever a charged conductor brought in contact with other conductor, charge continuously flows from one to another until their potential becomes equal. This is also called sharing of charges.

Conduction: The process of transfer of charge by contact of two conducting bodies is known as conduction.

(1) Contact is necessary

(2) Only conductors can be charged by this method

(3) In this method both conductors will acquire same nature of charge.

(4) Total charge of the system distributes in the ratio of their radii (only for spherical objects)

Consider two charged spheres $\left(\mathrm{q}_1, \mathrm{R}_1\right) \&\left(\mathrm{q}_2, \mathrm{R}_2\right)$  are connected by a wire or touched with each other.

After conduction let their final charges become  $Q_1 \& Q_2$ respectively then

$Q=q_1+q_2=Q_1+Q_2$

$\frac{Q_1}{Q_2}=\frac{R_1}{R_2}$

$\text { So, } Q_1=\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_2} Q$

$Q_2=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} Q$

Gold leaf electroscope : It is used to detect the presence of charge. When a conducting body touches the metal knob of an electroscope, then knob & leaves both wire acquire same nature of charge.

When a charged body is placed near the electroscope then knob will acquire opposite nature of charge & leaves will acquire same nature of charge.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Coulomb’s Law : The electrostatic force of interaction between two point charges is directly proportional to the magnitude of product of changes and inversely proportional to the square of distance between them.” This force always works along the line joining the two charges.

$\mathrm{F}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}$

$\mathrm{k}=\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}$

$\text { In SI system, } \mathrm{k}=9 \times 10^9 \dfrac{\mathrm{~N} \times \mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{C}^2}$

Where k = proportionality constant or coulomb’s constant or electrostatic constant

Value of k depends upon the choice of system of units.

$\epsilon_0=\text { permittivity of free space or vacuum }=8.85 \times 10^{-12} \dfrac{\mathrm{C}^2}{\mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{m}^2}$

When the point charge system is placed in a homogeneous dielectric medium.

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \in} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}_2}\\ &\epsilon=\text { permittivity of medium }=\epsilon_0 \epsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \end{aligned}$

$\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}=$ relative permittivity of medium or Dielectric constant of medium (K)

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 \epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}} \frac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\dfrac{1}{\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}\right) \Rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}\\ &\text { The value of } \epsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \text { or } K \geq 1 \text {, i.e. } F_m \leq F \end{aligned}$

Note :- Mutual force of interaction between charges is independent of medium.

For two charge system :

In both the cases shown - Net external force on the system is zero so linear momentum of system remains conserved.

For the system shown, line of action of force for both forces is same. So, net torque about any point for the system is zero.

Angular momentum = Constant

Vector form of Coulomb's Law :

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{12}=\text { force on } \mathrm{q}_1 \text { due to } \mathrm{q}_2=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2} \hat{\mathrm{r}}_{21}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^3} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{21}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{21}=\text { force on } \mathrm{q}_2 \text { due to } \mathrm{q}_1=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{12}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^3} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{12}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Equilibrium of suspended charge system (Pith Ball problems): Two identical charged pith balls are suspended by insulated strings of equal length, by a common point of suspension, if each ball has mass m then the problem related to it can be treated as

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T} \sin \theta=\mathrm{F_e}_{\mathrm{}} \\ & \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta=\mathrm{mg} \\ & \tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{mg}} \end{aligned}$

$\mathrm{r}=2 \ell \sin \theta$  (distance between charges, where $\ell$ is length of string)

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{4 \ell^2 \sin ^2 \theta}  \end{aligned}$

Case - 1 :$\text { If } q_1=q_2, m_1=m_2 \text {, then } \theta_1=\theta_2(\operatorname{say} \theta)$

Case - 2 : $\text { If } q_1 \neq q_2, m_1=m_2 \text {, then } \theta_1=\theta_2(\operatorname{say} \alpha)$

Case - 3: $\text { If } q_1=q_2, m_1 \neq m_2 \text {, then } \theta_1 \neq \theta_2$

$\text { If } \mathrm{m}_1>\mathrm{m}_2 \text { then } \theta_1<\theta_2$

Case -4 : If whole system placed in gravity free space $\text { (  } g=0 \text { ) }$

$\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{4 \mathrm{l}^2}$

$\text { Tension in thread } \mathrm{T}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq^2}}{4 \mathrm{l}^2}$

modules.name: Electric Dipole And Electric Field Lines

blocks.title: Electric Field Lines
blocks.text:
Electric Dipole : A system of two equal and opposite charges placed at very small separation is known as electric dipole.

Dipole Moment : The dipole moment of a dipole is equal to product of magnitude of either charge and separation between the charges.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{q} \vec{\ell}$

It is a vector quantity whose direction is from (-q) to (+q)

$\text { SI unit } \rightarrow \text { C-m, Practical unit } \rightarrow \text { debye }\left(3.33 \times 10^{-30} \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{m}\right)$

Electric Field Due to a short Dipole :

(1) At axial / End on position :

$\text { In vector form } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{axis}}=\left(\dfrac{2 \mathrm{kp}}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right) \hat{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{k \vec p}}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

(2) At Equator\Broad Side on position :

$\text { in vector from } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{k} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{r}^3}(-\hat{\mathrm{i}})$

(3) At General Position :

$\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kp}}{\mathrm{r}^3} \sqrt{(2 \cos \theta)^2+(\sin \theta)^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kp}}{\mathrm{r}^3} \sqrt{3 \cos ^2 \theta +1}$

$\tan \alpha=\dfrac{1}{2} \tan \theta$

Electric lines of electrostatic field have following properties :-

(1) Imaginary lines

(2) Never intersect each other

(3) Electrostatic field lines never forms closed loops

(4) Field lines ends or starts normally at the surface of a conductor.

(5) They originate from (+) charge and terminate at (-)charge.

(6) Number of electric field lines per unit area normal to the area at a point represents magnitude of intensity, crowded lines represent strong field while distant lines weak field.

(7) Tangent to the line of force at a point in an electric field gives the direction of intensity of electric field.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Electric Flux : This physical quantity is used to measure strength of electric field (also called flux density).

The electric flux can be understood graphically by the total number of electric field lines passing through an area.

$\text { Unit of flux : } \mathrm{Nm}^2 / \mathrm{C} \text { or Vm. }$

Flux is a scalar quantity.

$\text { Dimensional formula of } \phi \text { is }\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right] \text {. }$

Electric flux through a surface

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \phi=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \\ & \Rightarrow \phi=\mathrm{EA} \cos \theta\end{aligned}$

$\theta$ is the angle letween electric field $(\vec{E})$ and area vector $(\vec{A})$.

Gauss’s Law: Net electric flux passing through any closed imaginary surface (Gaussian surface) is $\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ times of the total charge enclosed by it.

$\phi_{\text {net }}=\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{dA}}=\dfrac{Q_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0}$

Note:

(1) Flux through Gaussian surface is independent of location of charges within Gaussian surface.

(2) Flux through Gaussian surface is independent of shape and size of Gaussian surface provided the net charge enclosed remains same.

(3)When net flux is going out then positive charge is enclosed by Gaussian surface

(4) When net flux is coming in then negative charge is enclosed by Gaussian surface

(5) In Gauss’s theorem

$\mathrm{E} \rightarrow \text { due to all the charges, but } \phi_{\text {closed }} \rightarrow \text { due to enclosed charges only. }$

(6) When an imaginary closed surface placed in an external electric field, net flux passing through it, will be zero.

(7) Gauss’s theorem is applicable for all the forces following inverse square law

(8) For a Gaussian surface  $\phi=0$ does not imply E = 0, but E = 0 implies  $\phi=0$.

Electrostatic Potential Energy (EPE) : EPE of a point charge, is the amount of work done in bringing the charge from infinity to the present position without changing its kinetic energy.

An object may have EPE by virtue of

(1) Its own charge called self-energy and

(2) Its relative position in the system of charges, called interaction energy.

Therefore, total EPE = self-energy + interaction energy

EPE is defined only for conservative field like gravitational field, electrostatic field etc.

Electrostatic Potential Energy (EPE) of two point charge system:

$\mathrm{U}-0=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQq}}{\mathrm{r}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQq}}{\mathrm{r}}$

$\text { As we consider infinity as reference \& } U_{\infty}=0$

Note: Always put sign of the charge in this formula.

Potential energy under repulsive forces is positive.

Potential energy under attractive forces is negative.

Amount of work done in changing the configuration of charge particles.

$\mathrm{W}=\Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{i}}$

Variation of U with r for two-point charge system :

Electrostatic Potential Energy of a System of Charges :

(1) For 3-point charge system :

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{S}}=\mathrm{U}_{12}+\mathrm{U}_{23}+\mathrm{U}_{31} \\ & \mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}_{12}}+\frac{\mathrm{kq}_2 \mathrm{q}_3}{\mathrm{r}_{23}}+\frac{\mathrm{kq}_3 \mathrm{q}_1}{\mathrm{r}_{31}} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}  &\text { Similarly, for } \mathrm{n} \text { point charge system }\\ &\text { No. of pairs }=\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \end{aligned}$

blocks.text:
Electric Potential : The work done by external agent in taking a unit point positive charge from a reference point (generally taken at infinity) to that point P without changing its kinetic energy.

If  $\left(\mathrm{W}_{\infty} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\right)_{\text {ext }}$  is the work required in moving a point charge $q_0$ from infinity to a point P, the electric potential of the point P is

$\left.V_p=\frac{\left(W_{\infty \rightarrow-p}\right)_{e x t}}{q}\right]_{\Delta K=0}$

It is scalar quantity

S.I. Unit of potential is volt =$\frac{\text { Joule }}{\text { coulomb }} $

and its dimensional formula is $\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{I}^{-1}\right] \text {. }$

Potential can be positive, negative and even zero. Hence charges must be taken with sign.

Electrostatic Potential due to a point charge

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{W}_{\infty \rightarrow \mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{q}_0}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQq}_0}{\mathrm{q}_0 \mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{r}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{r}}$

Potential due to a positive point charge $V_P=+\dfrac{k Q}{r}$

Potential due to a negative point charge $V_P=-\dfrac{k Q}{r}$

Electrostatic Potential due to a Uniformly Charged Ring:

(1) At the centre :

$V=\dfrac{k Q}{R}$

(2) On its axis :

$\mathrm{V}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{x}^2}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{r}}$

Electrostatic Potential due to a Uniformly Charged Circular Arc :

$V=\dfrac{k Q}{R}=\dfrac{k(\theta R \lambda)}{R}=k \theta \lambda$

Relation between electrostatic field (E) and potential (V):

$\vec{E}=-\vec{\nabla} V$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Force & Torque on Dipole in a Uniform Electric Field :

In uniform electric field both charges experience equal and opposite force, so net force on dipole is zero.

Torque/Couple of force = magnitude of either force × perpendicular distance between lines of force.

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{\tau}=(\mathrm{qE}) \mathrm{l} \sin \theta \text { or } \vec{\tau}=(\mathrm{ql}) \operatorname{Esin} \theta \\ & \vec{\tau}=\mathrm{pE} \sin \theta \text { or } \vec{\tau}=(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}) \end{aligned}$

Work done in rotating a dipole in uniform electric field :

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{pE}\left(\cos \theta_1-\cos \theta_2\right)$

Electric Potential due to Short Dipole :-

1.At axial point :

$V_p=\frac{k p}{r^2}$

2.At equatorial point :

$\mathrm{V_p}=\mathrm{V}_1+\mathrm{V}_2=\frac{\mathrm{kq}}{\mathrm{x}}-\frac{\mathrm{kq}}{\mathrm{x}}=0 \quad(\therefore \mathrm{~V}=0)$

3.Potential at general point (r, $\theta$):

$\begin{aligned} &\text { So, net potential at point } A, V=\frac{k(p \cos \theta)}{r^2}\\ &\therefore \quad \mathrm{V}=\frac{\mathrm{k}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{r}})}{\mathrm{r}^3} \quad(\text { here } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OA}}) \end{aligned}$

Potential Energy of dipole in electric field: $\vec{ E}$ is a conservative field so whatever work is done in rotating a dipole from $\theta_1 \text { to } \theta_2$  it is just equal to change in the electrostatic potential energy.

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{pE} \cos \theta \text { or } \mathrm{U}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} . \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} .$

$\text { Case-(i): When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \| \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \Rightarrow \theta=0^{\circ} \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{pE}=\mathrm{U}_{\min }$

$\text { ( } \because \text { Here } \mathrm{F}=0, \tau=0 \Rightarrow \text { Stable equilibrium) }$

$\text { Case-(ii): When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \perp \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \Rightarrow \theta=90^{\circ} \Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=0 \text { (reference position) }$

$(\because \text { Here } \mathrm{F}=0, \tau=\text { maximum }) \Rightarrow \text { Not in equilibrium }$

$\text { Case-(iii): When angle between } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \& \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \text { is } 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow U=+p E=U_{\max }$

$(\because \text { Here } \mathrm{F}=0, \tau=0) \Rightarrow \text { Unstable equilibrium }$

blocks.text:
Conductors and their Properties :-

1.Conductors are materials which contain large number of free electrons which can move freely inside the conductor.

(2. Electrostatic field lines never exist inside a conductor.

3.Electric field lines terminates & originates always perpendicular to the surface of conductor because the surface of conductor is an equipotential surface.

4.In electrostatics, conductors are always equipotential surfaces.

5.Charge always resides on the outer surface of a conductor.

6. If there is a cavity inside a charged conductor with the cavity devoid of any charge then charge will always reside only on the outer surface of the conductor.

7.Electric field intensity near a conducting surface is given by the formula

$\vec{E} = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} \hat{n}$

Concept of Earthing : Earth is conducting body with zero potential (assumed). When a charged body is connected to earth, charge flows continuously till potential of body becomes zero.

Leakage of Charge : Leakage of charge from sharp points of a conductor.

Leakage of charge from sharp points of a conductor

$\begin{aligned} & \text { Here } \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{B}} \text { but } \sigma_{\mathrm{B}}>\sigma_{\mathrm{A}}, \\ & \text { hence } \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}>\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{A}}\left\{\because \mathrm{E}=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\right\} \end{aligned}$

Thus charge density & hence electric field is larger at sharp corners as compared to flat surfaces due to their less radius of curvature.

$\sigma_1=\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}_1}{4 \pi \mathrm{R}_1^2} \& \sigma_2=\dfrac{\mathrm{Q}_2}{4 \pi \mathrm{R}_2^2} \quad \because \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}_1}{\mathrm{Q}_2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1} \Rightarrow \sigma \propto \dfrac{1}{\mathrm{R}}$

Electrostatic Shielding :

• Electrostatic shielding is the method of protecting a certain region from the effect of electric field.
    • A cavity surrounded by conducting walls is a field free region as long as there are no charges inside the cavity.
Sharing of charges :  When two charged conductors are connected by a conducting wire then charge flows between then till stops when the potential of both conductors become equal.

$\mathrm{V}=\dfrac{\mathrm{k} \mathrm{Q}_1}{\mathrm{R}_1}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}_2}{\mathrm{R}_2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{Q}_1}{\mathrm{Q}_2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2} \quad \text { or } \quad \mathrm{Q}_1=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2}\right) \mathrm{Q} \text { or } \mathrm{Q}_2=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{R}_2}{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2}\right) \mathrm{Q} \quad\left\{\mathrm{Q}_1+\mathrm{Q}_2=\mathrm{Q}\right\}$

Coulomb’s Law : The electrostatic force of interaction between two point charges is directly proportional to the magnitude of product of changes and inversely proportional to the square of distance between them.” This force always works along the line joining the two charges.

$\mathrm{F}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}$

$\mathrm{k}=\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}$

$\text { In SI system, } \mathrm{k}=9 \times 10^9 \dfrac{\mathrm{~N} \times \mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{C}^2}$

Where k = proportionality constant or coulomb’s constant or electrostatic constant

Value of k depends upon the choice of system of units.

$\epsilon_0=\text { permittivity of free space or vacuum }=8.85 \times 10^{-12} \dfrac{\mathrm{C}^2}{\mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{m}^2}$

When the point charge system is placed in a homogeneous dielectric medium.

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \in} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}_2}\\ &\epsilon=\text { permittivity of medium }=\epsilon_0 \epsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \end{aligned}$

$\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}=$ relative permittivity of medium or Dielectric constant of medium (K)

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 \epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}} \frac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\dfrac{1}{\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}\left(\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2}\right) \Rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}\\ &\text { The value of } \epsilon_{\mathrm{r}} \text { or } K \geq 1 \text {, i.e. } F_m \leq F \end{aligned}$

Note :- Mutual force of interaction between charges is independent of medium.

For two charge system :

In both the cases shown - Net external force on the system is zero so linear momentum of system remains conserved.

For the system shown, line of action of force for both forces is same. So, net torque about any point for the system is zero.

Angular momentum = Constant

Vector form of Coulomb's Law :

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{12}=\text { force on } \mathrm{q}_1 \text { due to } \mathrm{q}_2=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2} \hat{\mathrm{r}}_{21}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^3} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{21}$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{21}=\text { force on } \mathrm{q}_2 \text { due to } \mathrm{q}_1=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{12}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}_1 \mathrm{q}_2}{\mathrm{r}^3} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}_{12}$

Equilibrium of suspended charge system (Pith Ball problems): Two identical charged pith balls are suspended by insulated strings of equal length, by a common point of suspension, if each ball has mass m then the problem related to it can be treated as

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{T} \sin \theta=\mathrm{F_e}_{\mathrm{}} \\ & \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta=\mathrm{mg} \\ & \tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}}{\mathrm{mg}} \end{aligned}$

$\mathrm{r}=2 \ell \sin \theta$  (distance between charges, where $\ell$ is length of string)

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{4 \ell^2 \sin ^2 \theta}  \end{aligned}$

Case - 1 :$\text { If } q_1=q_2, m_1=m_2 \text {, then } \theta_1=\theta_2(\operatorname{say} \theta)$

Case - 2 : $\text { If } q_1 \neq q_2, m_1=m_2 \text {, then } \theta_1=\theta_2(\operatorname{say} \alpha)$

Case - 3: $\text { If } q_1=q_2, m_1 \neq m_2 \text {, then } \theta_1 \neq \theta_2$

$\text { If } \mathrm{m}_1>\mathrm{m}_2 \text { then } \theta_1<\theta_2$

Case -4 : If whole system placed in gravity free space $\text { (  } g=0 \text { ) }$

$\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{\mathrm{r}^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq}^2}{4 \mathrm{l}^2}$

$\text { Tension in thread } \mathrm{T}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq^2}}{4 \mathrm{l}^2}$

Electrostatic Equilibrium : In physics if a particle or system is in equilibrium means net force on particle or system is zero.

Short Trick: - For force on charge q to be zero

It is defined as the net force experienced by a unit positive test charge.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}}{\mathrm{q}_0} \text { SI unit : } \mathrm{N} / \mathrm{C} \text { or } \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{m}$

Test Charge : It is a charge of very small magnitude which do not produce significant electric field.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\lim _{\mathrm{q}_0 \rightarrow 0}\left(\dfrac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~F}}}{\mathrm{q}_0}\right) .$

  • Force on a point charge is in the same direction as that of electric field on positive charge and in opposite direction as that of electric field on a negative charge.
Note: - K is dielectric constant of medium also known as relative permittivity of medium.

$\text { (In general } \mathrm{K} \geq 1 \text { so } \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{m}} \leq \mathrm{E} \text { ) }$

Special Cases :-

blocks.title: Electric Field Lines
blocks.text:
Electric Dipole : A system of two equal and opposite charges placed at very small separation is known as electric dipole.

Dipole Moment : The dipole moment of a dipole is equal to product of magnitude of either charge and separation between the charges.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{q} \vec{\ell}$

It is a vector quantity whose direction is from (-q) to (+q)

$\text { SI unit } \rightarrow \text { C-m, Practical unit } \rightarrow \text { debye }\left(3.33 \times 10^{-30} \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{m}\right)$

Electric Field Due to a short Dipole :

(1) At axial / End on position :

$\text { In vector form } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{axis}}=\left(\dfrac{2 \mathrm{kp}}{\mathrm{r}^3}\right) \hat{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{k \vec p}}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

(2) At Equator\Broad Side on position :

$\text { in vector from } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{k} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{r}^3}(-\hat{\mathrm{i}})$

(3) At General Position :

$\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kp}}{\mathrm{r}^3} \sqrt{(2 \cos \theta)^2+(\sin \theta)^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kp}}{\mathrm{r}^3} \sqrt{3 \cos ^2 \theta +1}$

$\tan \alpha=\dfrac{1}{2} \tan \theta$

Electric lines of electrostatic field have following properties :-

(1) Imaginary lines

(2) Never intersect each other

(3) Electrostatic field lines never forms closed loops

(4) Field lines ends or starts normally at the surface of a conductor.

(5) They originate from (+) charge and terminate at (-)charge.

(6) Number of electric field lines per unit area normal to the area at a point represents magnitude of intensity, crowded lines represent strong field while distant lines weak field.

(7) Tangent to the line of force at a point in an electric field gives the direction of intensity of electric field.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Electric Flux : This physical quantity is used to measure strength of electric field (also called flux density).

The electric flux can be understood graphically by the total number of electric field lines passing through an area.

$\text { Unit of flux : } \mathrm{Nm}^2 / \mathrm{C} \text { or Vm. }$

Flux is a scalar quantity.

$\text { Dimensional formula of } \phi \text { is }\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right] \text {. }$

Electric flux through a surface

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \phi=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \\ & \Rightarrow \phi=\mathrm{EA} \cos \theta\end{aligned}$

$\theta$ is the angle letween electric field $(\vec{E})$ and area vector $(\vec{A})$.

Gauss’s Law: Net electric flux passing through any closed imaginary surface (Gaussian surface) is $\dfrac{1}{\varepsilon_0}$ times of the total charge enclosed by it.

$\phi_{\text {net }}=\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{dA}}=\dfrac{Q_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0}$

Note:

(1) Flux through Gaussian surface is independent of location of charges within Gaussian surface.

(2) Flux through Gaussian surface is independent of shape and size of Gaussian surface provided the net charge enclosed remains same.

(3)When net flux is going out then positive charge is enclosed by Gaussian surface

(4) When net flux is coming in then negative charge is enclosed by Gaussian surface

(5) In Gauss’s theorem

$\mathrm{E} \rightarrow \text { due to all the charges, but } \phi_{\text {closed }} \rightarrow \text { due to enclosed charges only. }$

(6) When an imaginary closed surface placed in an external electric field, net flux passing through it, will be zero.

(7) Gauss’s theorem is applicable for all the forces following inverse square law

(8) For a Gaussian surface  $\phi=0$ does not imply E = 0, but E = 0 implies  $\phi=0$.

Applications of Gauss’s Law :

(i) Electric field due to a uniformly charged long wire :

$\mathrm{E}(2 \pi \mathrm{rL})=\dfrac{\lambda \mathrm{L}}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{\lambda}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{r}} \text { or } \mathrm{E}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{k} \lambda}{\mathrm{r}}$

(2) Electric Field due to Uniformly Charged Infinite Sheet :

(i) Non conducting sheet :

$\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0}$

Electric field due to non conducting sheet is uniform

(ii) Conducting sheet or metal plate :

$\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$

Electric field due to conducting sheet is uniform

Electric field due to the charged conducting sphere and non conducting sphere

(1) Electric field due to point charge :

$\text { From } E\left(4 \pi r^2\right)=\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow E=\dfrac{q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^2} \text { or } \dfrac{k q}{r^2}$

(2) Electric field due to uniformly charged thin shell or conducting sphere.

(a) EF at any point outside the sphere (r>R)

$\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0\left(\mathrm{r}^2\right)} \text { or } \mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq}}{\mathrm{r}^2}$

(b) EF at any point lying on the surface of sphere (r = R)

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{S}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 \mathrm{R}^2}=\dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} \quad\left(\because \sigma=\dfrac{q}{4 \pi \mathrm{R}^2}\right)$

(3) EF at any point inside the sphere (r < R)

$\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{in}}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{ds}}=\dfrac{0}{\varepsilon_0} \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{in}}=0$

Variation of E with r :

(4) Electric field due to uniformly charged nonconducting sphere :

(a) EF at any point outside the sphere (r > R) :

$\mathrm{E}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kq}}{\mathrm{r}^2}$

Thus for point lying outside the sphere, sphere behaves as point charge centered at centre.

(b) EF at any point lying on the surface of sphere (r=R) :

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{S}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{R}^2}=\dfrac{\mathrm{qR}}{3\left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^3\right) \varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{\rho \mathrm{R}}{3 \epsilon_0}$

$\text { [ } \therefore \rho \text { is volume charge density] }$

(c) EF at any point inside the sphere (r<R)

$\mathrm{E}_{\text {in }}=\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \dfrac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{R}^3}(\mathrm{r})=\dfrac{\mathrm{q}}{3\left(\dfrac{4}{3} \pi \mathrm{R}^3\right)}(\mathrm{r})=\dfrac{\rho}{3 \varepsilon_0}(\mathrm{r})$

For r = 0, E = 0 $\rightarrow$  electric field intensity at the centre of the sphere is zero.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Electric Potential : The work done by external agent in taking a unit point positive charge from a reference point (generally taken at infinity) to that point P without changing its kinetic energy.

If  $\left(\mathrm{W}_{\infty} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\right)_{\text {ext }}$  is the work required in moving a point charge $q_0$ from infinity to a point P, the electric potential of the point P is

$\left.V_p=\frac{\left(W_{\infty \rightarrow-p}\right)_{e x t}}{q}\right]_{\Delta K=0}$

It is scalar quantity

S.I. Unit of potential is volt =$\frac{\text { Joule }}{\text { coulomb }} $

and its dimensional formula is $\left[\mathrm{M}^1 \mathrm{~L}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{I}^{-1}\right] \text {. }$

Potential can be positive, negative and even zero. Hence charges must be taken with sign.

Electrostatic Potential due to a point charge

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{W}_{\infty \rightarrow \mathrm{P}}}{\mathrm{q}_0}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQq}_0}{\mathrm{q}_0 \mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{r}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~V}_{\mathrm{p}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{r}}$

Potential due to a positive point charge $V_P=+\dfrac{k Q}{r}$

Potential due to a negative point charge $V_P=-\dfrac{k Q}{r}$

Electrostatic Potential due to a Uniformly Charged Ring:

(1) At the centre :

$V=\dfrac{k Q}{R}$

(2) On its axis :

$\mathrm{V}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^2+\mathrm{x}^2}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{r}}$

Electrostatic Potential due to a Uniformly Charged Circular Arc :

$V=\dfrac{k Q}{R}=\dfrac{k(\theta R \lambda)}{R}=k \theta \lambda$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Relation between electrostatic field (E) and potential (V):

$\vec{E}=-\vec{\nabla} V$

So, negative gradient of electric potential is equal to electric field.

Since electric field is negative gradient of potential, thus potential decreases in the direction of $\vec{E}$

Case(1):Finding E when V is given:

$\begin{aligned}  & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=-\frac{\partial V}{\partial \mathrm{x}} \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial \mathrm{y}} \hat{\mathrm{j}}-\frac{\partial V}{\partial \mathrm{z}} \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\mathrm{E}_y \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{z}} \hat{\mathrm{k}} \end{aligned}$

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}}=-\frac{\partial \mathrm{V}}{\partial \mathrm{x}} ; \quad \mathrm{E}_y=-\frac{\partial \mathrm{V}}{\partial \mathrm{y}} ; \quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{z}}=-\frac{\partial \mathrm{V}}{\partial \mathrm{z}}$

Case(2): Finding V when E is given :

$\because E=-\frac{d V}{d r} \Rightarrow d V=-E d r \Rightarrow d V=-\vec{E} . d \vec{r} \quad \text { where } d \vec{r}=d x \hat{i}+d y \hat{j}+d z \hat{k}$

On integration

$\Delta V=V_p-V_{r e f}=-\int_{r e f}^{\mathrm{p}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{dr}}$

$\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{p}}-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{ref}}=-\int_{\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{ref}}}^{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{p}}} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{dx}-\int_{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{ref}}}^{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{p}}} \mathrm{E}_y \mathrm{dy}-\int_{Z_{\text {ref }}}^{Z_{\mathrm{p}}} \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{z}} \mathrm{dz} .$

Note: In uniform electric field

$ \Delta V=E d$

P.D. = E (distance between two points along electric field)

Electrostatic Potential due to a Charged Conducting Sphere or Spherical Shell :

(1) For outside points (r > R)

$V_{out}=\dfrac{k Q}{r}=\dfrac{\sigma R^2}{\varepsilon_0 r}$

(2) For points on the surface (r = R)

$\mathrm{V_s}=\dfrac{\sigma \mathrm{R}}{\varepsilon_0}=\dfrac{\mathrm{kQ}}{\mathrm{R}}$

(3) For Inside points (r < R)

$V_{in}=\dfrac{k Q}{R}$

Variation of potential with r :

Electric Potential due to Uniformly Charged Non-conducting Sphere :

(1) Outside (r > R)

$V_{out}=\dfrac{K Q}{r}$

(2) On the surface (r = R)

$\mathrm{V_{surface}} =\dfrac{\mathrm{KQ}}{\mathrm{R}}$

(3) Inside (r < R)

$\operatorname{V_{in}}=\dfrac{K Q}{2 R^3}\left[3 R^2-r^2\right]$

At center, r = 0

$\mathrm{V}_{\text {c}}=\dfrac{3}{2} \frac{\mathrm{KQ}}{\mathrm{R}}=\dfrac{3}{2} \mathrm{~V}_{\text {surface }}$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Charge Particle Projected Perpendicular to Uniform Electric Field : When the charge particle is projected perpendicular to a uniform electric field $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{u}} \perp \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}})$

$\mathrm{y}=\left(\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{\mathrm{qE}}{\mathrm{mu}^2}\right) \mathrm{x}^2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{y}=\mathrm{kx}^2 \text { (parabolic path) }$

$\begin{aligned} &\text { Velocity of particle at time ' } t \text { ' }\\ &$$\begin{aligned} & \vec{v}=v_x \hat{i}+v_y \hat{j} \\ & \vec{v}=u \hat{i}+\left(\frac{q E}{m} t\right) \hat{j} \end{aligned}$$ \end{aligned}$$

$\text { Speed, } v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2} \text { and in diagram } \tan \alpha=\dfrac{v_y}{v_x}$

where $\alpha$ is angle of deviation.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Force & Torque on Dipole in a Uniform Electric Field :

In uniform electric field both charges experience equal and opposite force, so net force on dipole is zero.

Torque/Couple of force = magnitude of either force × perpendicular distance between lines of force.

$\begin{aligned} & \vec{\tau}=(\mathrm{qE}) \mathrm{l} \sin \theta \text { or } \vec{\tau}=(\mathrm{ql}) \operatorname{Esin} \theta \\ & \vec{\tau}=\mathrm{pE} \sin \theta \text { or } \vec{\tau}=(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}) \end{aligned}$

Work done in rotating a dipole in uniform electric field :

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{pE}\left(\cos \theta_1-\cos \theta_2\right)$

Electric Potential due to Short Dipole :-

1.At axial point :

$V_p=\frac{k p}{r^2}$

2.At equatorial point :

$\mathrm{V_p}=\mathrm{V}_1+\mathrm{V}_2=\frac{\mathrm{kq}}{\mathrm{x}}-\frac{\mathrm{kq}}{\mathrm{x}}=0 \quad(\therefore \mathrm{~V}=0)$

3.Potential at general point (r, $\theta$):

$\begin{aligned} &\text { So, net potential at point } A, V=\frac{k(p \cos \theta)}{r^2}\\ &\therefore \quad \mathrm{V}=\frac{\mathrm{k}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \cdot \hat{\mathrm{r}})}{\mathrm{r}^3} \quad(\text { here } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OA}}) \end{aligned}$

Potential Energy of dipole in electric field: $\vec{ E}$ is a conservative field so whatever work is done in rotating a dipole from $\theta_1 \text { to } \theta_2$  it is just equal to change in the electrostatic potential energy.

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{pE} \cos \theta \text { or } \mathrm{U}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} . \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} .$

$\text { Case-(i): When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \| \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \Rightarrow \theta=0^{\circ} \quad \Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{pE}=\mathrm{U}_{\min }$

$\text { ( } \because \text { Here } \mathrm{F}=0, \tau=0 \Rightarrow \text { Stable equilibrium) }$

$\text { Case-(ii): When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \perp \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \Rightarrow \theta=90^{\circ} \Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=0 \text { (reference position) }$

$(\because \text { Here } \mathrm{F}=0, \tau=\text { maximum }) \Rightarrow \text { Not in equilibrium }$

$\text { Case-(iii): When angle between } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \& \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \text { is } 180^{\circ} \Rightarrow U=+p E=U_{\max }$

$(\because \text { Here } \mathrm{F}=0, \tau=0) \Rightarrow \text { Unstable equilibrium }$
